purpose: Rejected experiment: replace PgfMacroBlock's three duplicated byte-at-a-time significance-flag scans (`while (!sigFlagVector[sigEnd]) sigEnd++;`, appearing in ComposeBitplane and both ComposeBitplaneRld overloads) with a single shared FindNextSignificant(start) helper that reinterprets the bool[] backing array as byte[] (MemoryMarshal.Cast<bool, byte>) and delegates to the BCL's hardware-accelerated ReadOnlySpan<byte>.IndexOf((byte)1) - a pure 'find next set byte' memory search, distinct from BitplaneDecode's inherently sequential bit-level entropy decoding (which stays untouched). Motivated by a fresh look at the existing baseline .diagsession profile (docs/benchmarks/pgfcodec/2026-08-06-445451b-session-workload-baseline's incidental capture, re-examined per the user's explicit request to keep mining it for non-memory optimization candidates): PgfMacroBlock.BitplaneDecode is the largest real (non-harness) codec hotspot in that trace (69 of 739 dotnet-process exclusive samples, second only to PgfImageDecoder.TryDecode's 87 samples - which is inlined SessionWorkloadBenchmarks.Checksum harness code per the skill's own 'distinguish codec work from benchmark-harness work' guardrail, not a real candidate). This sigFlagVector scan was chosen over further BitplaneDecode SIMD attempts because, unlike the bitstream decode itself, it is a genuine, safe, portable memory-search pattern already solved by the BCL.
methodology: Matched-conditions comparison, not a cross-session reuse: `git stash push -- source/PictTag.PgfCodec/PgfMacroBlock.cs` isolated the change, then before (stashed/original) and after (popped/changed) MediumRun (N=15, LaunchCount=2) benchmarks were run back-to-back on the same machine/session to avoid the confound seen in an earlier, less careful comparison against a different session's archived baseline (which showed one variant at -3%, not reproduced here).
result: REJECTED - functionally correct but no measurable end-to-end improvement. Full codec suite (1393/1393, all pre-existing native-oracle/round-trip tests, no new tests needed since the change is a pure internal search-mechanism swap with identical output) and the Browser/WASM build were green. MediumRun (AMD Ryzen 7 5800X), matched conditions: DecodeFiftyImagesInNewSession(False) 121.8ms -> 121.7ms (-0.08%); ProgressiveDecodeFiftyImagesInNewSession(False) 132.9ms -> 133.8ms (+0.68%); DecodeFiftyImagesInNewSession(True) 136.7ms -> 137.2ms (+0.37%); ProgressiveDecodeFiftyImagesInNewSession(True) 150.3ms -> 148.6ms (-1.13%). All four deltas are within each run's own StdDev band, with no consistent direction across the four rows (2 up, 2 down) - a clean 'no effect' result, not a borderline one. Root cause assessment: the original scalar loop (`while (!sigFlagVector[sigEnd]) sigEnd++;`) is already about as cheap as a loop can be for RyuJIT - one bounds-checked byte load, one compare, one increment, no function-call overhead - and the JIT likely already keeps it in registers with good branch prediction (the loop body itself never branches unpredictably; it just walks until non-zero). The BCL's vectorized IndexOf carries its own per-call overhead (byte alignment checks, vector-width dispatch) that is only worthwhile for scan lengths long enough to amortize it; per the pre-implementation reasoning in this same file's docstring, most individual scans in this algorithm are short (denser bitplanes mean the gap between consecutive already-significant positions is typically small), so the fixed per-call vectorization overhead cancels out the per-element savings on the very case that dominates by call count. Reverted (git checkout --); PgfMacroBlock.cs is unchanged from 937d052. Do not retry this specific IndexOf-based approach without evidence that a specific workload has long insignificant runs (e.g. very sparse/low-detail images at early bitplanes) where the fixed per-call cost would actually be amortized - the SessionWorkloadBenchmarks fixture set does not exercise that shape.
